newsitem.title: FRANCE: France readies paratroops for Zaire aid mission.
newsitem.headline: France readies paratroops for Zaire aid mission.

text.p: France is prepared to send 600 paratroopers to Zaire within 24 hours of U.N. approval for a multinational force to help starving refugees and have 600 more there a day later, defence officials said on Wednesday.

The sole remaining obstacle to the French soldiers' departure was final United Nations action after Washington agreed in principle to contribute troops to the mission, as Paris had insisted, the French Foreign Ministry said.

"France welcomes this (U.S.) decision, which will enable the force to get off the ground without delay and dispatch humanitarian aid to those people who are in distress," the ministry said in a statement.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette discussed details of the operation with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who was in Paris on Thursday for a conference on Bosnia.

"We were pleased to note that following the decision just announced by President Clinton, the international community is now ready to intervene for humanitarian purposes to aid these 1.2 million refugees and displaced people," de Charette told a joint news conference.
De Charette also planned to confer with Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy. Canada has agreed to lead the multinational force.
French army officers said the French detachment which could go within 24 hours was from the Eighth Marine Infantry Parachute Regiment (8th RPIMa) based in Castres, southwestern France.

The unit recently served in ex-Yugoslavia and in Africa itself, restoring order and shoring up a government allied to Paris when the local army mutinied in the Central African Republic earlier this year.

The second 600 men, who could be in Zaire within 48 hours of receiving orders, would be drawn from a sister regiment, the 3rd RPIMa, also made up of professionals with vast experience in Africa, the officers said.
"In fact, such detachments are always ready. It's a coincidence that this time the first and second wave units are particularly well adapted to the mission," one officer said.
The troops would be flown from France with weapons, rations and ammunition for several days under an existing alert system.

Armoured personnel carriers, if needed, could be flown in from the Central African Republic, the officers said. They declined comment when asked if helicopter gunships would be available to provide cover for humanitarian supply convoys.

Officials were also vague about where the proposed multinational force would muster. But they said Entebbe airport in Uganda or one of two French airfields in the Central African Republic could be the main base for the operation and the airlift of equipment and supplies required for the mission.
They said much still remained to be determined, including the precise mission at hand and especially the whereabouts of up the Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans.
"No one knows what's happening in the field. It's the rainy season and even American satellites are useless. Until we send scouts there, we won't know," one officer said.
He denied that a light aircraft which flew over Goma airfield on Wednesday drawing Tutsi rebel fire was a French military aircraft.
The officer played down opposition from the Tutsis to a French presence in the proposed force, saying France's position in the area was better than generally reported by the media.

Rwanda and the Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels have voiced opposition to French military involvement in the operation, accusing Paris of backing the former Hutu rulers in Rwanda who were overthrown in 1994 after a massacre of Tutsis.
Most of the refugees in eastern Zaire are Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994.
